Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege. One of the qualifications for becoming a member of this house is to be a Canadian citizen. I am a Canadian by naturalization. I am now apprehensive, Mr. Speaker, that the rights of members of parliament who are Canadian citizens by naturalization, and the rights of every other naturalized Canadian, are being seriously encroached upon by one of the provincial legislatures.
Second reading is now being debated by the Quebec legislature of a bill which tends to create a distinction between citizens of Canada; that is, between those who are Canadians by birth and those who are Canadian by naturalization. This is being done by amending the provincial election act to compel Canadian citizens by naturalization to produce their citizenship certificate before voting.
If anything was ever out of order, Mr. Speaker, this statement is.

If the hon. member will have patience for a moment or two, he will see my point of personal privilege.
This is a discrimination between Canadian citizens by naturalization and native-born Canadian citizens who are not obliged, under the proposed arrangement, to produce their birth certificates before voting.
I consider it to be an encroachment upon my status as a member of this house and I believe that steps should be taken, or that a statement should be made, to provide that provincial legislation cannot and should not differentiate between the rights of citizens of Canada, inasmuch as the status of citizenship is a matter which falls wholly within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament.

The hon. member for Nanaimo in question 12 asks the amount that has been expended and the estimated cost of Operation Pine

Tree, by which I assume he refers to the general radar defence system of Canada.
As every Canadian bomber pilot knows, one of the things first in importance for effective bombing is to be able to locate and know everything possible about the enemy's radar defence.
This information is useful for a number of reasons. With it, attacking bombers can take the line of approach where radar coverage is least effective. If the attacker has sufficient knowledge of the location and character of the radar defences, he can try to put them out of action by jamming, by bombing and by sabotage. For these reasons, actual or potential enemy forces go to great lengths to obtain this information.
Giving the cost of various stations would help an enemy to decide whether or not each station was simply an early warning station or whether it was also a station for ground-controlled interception, a very important thing for him to know.
Also, giving the amounts expended and the estimated costs of several stations would enable an enemy to estimate with pretty fair accuracy the degree of readiness and the time when each station and the complete system would be in full operation. It would also enable him to say how long it would take to build additional radar defences, should a new type of aircraft or other new feature increase the threat of bombing attack.
The radar defences of North America are planned and will be operated jointly by the United States and Canada, and the United States air force and the R.C.A.F. agreed that the numbers and names of sites and stations, the equipment, the progress of construction and operational data would not be revealed.
Some time ago I addressed a letter to representatives of the newspapers across Canada asking their co-operation in this and generally speaking that co-operation has been forthcoming.
There is another reason why such information should not be given officially by the government. Giving it would enable a potential enemy to assess the accuracy and efficiency of this system of intelligence.
For these and other reasons which might be mentioned, it is not considered to be in the public interest to give information that would assist a potential enemy in obtaining information of this character about our radar defences. The minister's statement
was a rather brief one and I think that perhaps as the discussion progresses he will have to amplify his remarks with respect to some of the provisions of the bill to be introduced. This resolution envisages the introduction of a bill to amend the Post Office Act, which by the way was amended in 1951. On the surface the resolution indicates some confusion with respect to the provisions of the prospective bill. The Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) indicates in the resolution that he desires to have legislative powers to enter into contracts for conveying mail involving an annual expenditure of $1,000 or less without tender. In view of the legislation amending the Post Office Act which was passed by the house and assented to on the 30th of June, 1951, and more particularly section 23, subsection 1, thereof, it would seem to me that the resolution is a move to reimplement legislation which has been passed by the parliament of Canada previously. I say that because I find that section 23 of the amended Post Office Act of 1951 contains these words:
When the Postmaster General conceives that the public interest will be promoted by such a course, he may enter into contracts for conveying mail involving an annual expenditure of $1,000 or less, if the amount to be paid for the services to be performed under the contract does not exceed the amount ordinarily paid for services of a like nature under contracts made after inviting tenders.
I realize that the resolution is in general terms and that when the bill is before us we may have a clearer idea of the difference between the section I have read, which was passed in 1951, and the prospective legislation to be introduced when the resolution carries. However, as it appears at the moment the indication is that what the government is doing is asking for legislation similar in terms to that passed at the session two years

ago. In addition, there is a new provision which we will know more about when the legislation comes before us in bill form. The intent of it is that under certain conditions, while a contract is still in force, the Postmaster General may increase the amount payable thereunder during the unexpired term thereof. The resolution is of course delightfully vague with respect to whether the reference is to contracts of $1,000 or less or to the entire gamut of contracts regardless of the amount of the accepted tender. Those are matters concerning which we will have to have further information as we proceed with the discussion of the resolution and when the bill comes before the house.
At this stage I should like to make a few random remarks with respect to the proposed legislation. During the war years, when the rural mail carrier was having great difficulties, as he has been for many years, the government hit upon a plan under the War Measures Act of introducing a system of supplementary payments for mail carriers. It was meant as an emergency measure and was implemented on a partial scale across Canada and made applicable to various routes throughout the country. The effect of it was that where the annual mileage rate for a rural mail route-I am calling on my memory at this time to be my witness and I am afraid one's memory is not always a very good witness-was less than $50 a mile the matter would be reviewed by the department. One difficulty that arose came about because, instead of notifying each rural mail carrier across Canada and telling him of the provision under which he was entitled to apply, to the best of my knowledge not a single rural mail carrier anywhere was notified directly by anybody in the Post Office Department with respect to what his rights were and what he was entitled to receive under the supplementary payments legislation.
The result was that across Canada there must have been not hundreds but thousands of rural mail contractors who missed out, if you like, on the benefits available under that provision. Some members of parliament and others, possibly those in the rural mail carriers' association, did notify some mail carriers as best they could but in a haphazard and hit-and-miss way. There was by no means full coverage. The result was that those who got attention from their members of parliament, from the rural mail carriers' association or from some other quarter, were the ones who received an increase in their contracts, and the other poor fellows, who did not seem to have any friends at court and who never learned anything about the provision, carried on at the old rate. When they made application afterwards to have the
Post Office Act
provision made retroactive so that the mistake could be rectified they were told by the government that it was [DOT] too late then, that the money had gone into the treasury of Canada, and of course no mere rural mail carrier could be allowed to tamper with anything so sacred as that. An obvious and serious injustice was done to many mail carriers from coast to coast.
That was the first stage. Later further supplementary payments were provided for under emergency legislation after the war ended. Then for a time supplementary payments went out of existence altogether. What the rural mail carrier has always been anxious to do is to get some redress for the almost impossible situation in which he finds himself as a carrier of Her Majesty's mail. When other people do business for Her Majesty and do various things for the government not very many of them have to put up with a tender system under which they have to come back every few years to find out first of all whether the government wants them. In the second place, they are faced with a situation where they have to try to get their tenders low enough so that they will be accepted. The result is that, while people in other branches of the Post Office Department have a regular and orderly method of employment, the rural mail carrier has not.
Over the years a number of members of parliament have called for a committee, and it has not always been those on one side of the house because I think throughout Canada and in the House of Commons there is a desire to see that the rural mail carriers get a very much better deal than they have in the past. I believe it is five or six years now since I first asked on the floor of the house that a committee be set up to deal with their problems. Later the request was enlarged to include the whole of the ramifications of the Post Office Department. I have received various answers as to why it could not be done. None of them were very convincing. Of course, no argument of the government necessarily convinces a member of the opposition the first time it is made.

I have said that I agree with the need and approve of the general principle contained in the resolution. I want to add one word of admonition or advice. What is being done will be acceptable to hon. members not only on this side but on all sides of the house and to the Canadian people as a whole. I shall say only a few words in order to clarify the situation because I believe that a little confusion has arisen. First of all, I must thank the members who have already spoken and who are ready to co-operate in this matter. The bill to be introduced amending the Post Office Act does not change the act at all except in those respects mentioned in the resolution. The purpose is to allow the Postmaster General to readjust the remuneration received by mail contractors. Some of my hon. friends complained about patronage and said in support of their complaints that we must maintain the tender system. We are keeping the tender system. Nothing in the law is changed so far as the tender system is concerned.
Someone said that we do not actually operate the tender system in respect of contracts under $1,000. That is true. According to the

law the department has the power to enter into contracts when the amount involved is under $1,000, but I would say that in 95 per cent ot all contracts under $1,000 the procedure is the same in that tenders are submitted by contractors. There has been a general complaint from all sides of the house that provision should be made to readjust the remuneration paid under mail contracts. I can remember my hon. friend (Mr. McLure) referring many times to a contractor in his riding who had submitted a tender $5 less than the other man but lost the contract. He said that the man had had experience, had expended money to buy a car, and that it was an injustice to him. This is one of the injustices we want to correct by the bill to be introduced.
Take, for instance, a contractor who has carried out his contract for three years and ten months. We would be ready now, as we have the power to do, and as was suggested by my hon. friend who spoke a few minutes ago, to renew his contract. If he has given good service, if he has gone to the expenditure of a considerable amount of money, and is obliged to submit a tender again, we do not see why we should not renew that contract. It is permissible to do so now, but on the other hand we do not want to oblige that man to renew the contract if he is certain of losing money. That is why the bill is to be brought forward. The purpose is to find a way to readjust the amount paid to the contractor in such circumstances so that he can continue to serve his country and not lose money while doing so.
At the present time we have the power to readjust the amount of money in contracts under $1,000 but the method of doing so is not very satisfactory. It is done by taking the average of similar contracts obtained by tenders in an area. We take the average. I do not want to go into the details. It will be up to the committee to find the best way to do it. We think that the plan on which the department has worked will give satisfaction to the committee. We want to be in a position to readjust not only contracts under $1,000 but all contracts with the exception of those mentioned in article 29 having to do with the railroads, Trans-Canada Air Lines and so on. If it is a good principle to adjust contracts, the amounts of which are under $1,000, it is equally just, if we can find a way to do so without discrimination, for all contracts of a similar nature whatever amount of money is involved.
The hon. member for Lake CeiSfc't^Teferred to the association. We have received constant demands from many sources over the last five

concerned. I must say at this stage that I have not particularly noticed any political patronage so far as the awarding of contracts for the carriage of mail is concerned, possibly partly due to the fact that the remuneration the department pays is low in relation to the average earnings of the working people in my constituency. But it is a difficult country to cover; it presents some unusual problems. Rural mail is carried by bus, by car, by truck, by barge, by launch and by steamer. For a short time it was carried by air to two isolated points as an experiment, which proved unsuccessful.
I have had a long residence in that district, and I have noticed the particular difficulties that the carrying of rural mail presents. However, I want to be fair. I have discussed this matter with the minister's officials, and I fully realize the difficult problem it is. But the tender system is not entirely satisfactory, and I know the mileage system presents difficulties. Even a salary system presents difficulties. That is why I welcome this committee which will have an opportunity to go into all these questions and into the experience of the officials of the department, and I trust that the rural mail couriers will have their representatives there to present their views. That is very important.
I want to give just briefly, Mr. Speaker, some examples of the unfairness that does exist under the tender system. I think of my district and of a certain workingman who had a small truck. He secured the mail contract between two points about a hundred miles apart. He gave most efficient service; he was well liked in the district. He was courteous, and usually kept the deliveries on time, sometimes under very difficult winter conditions. Then a tender was called for, and a man already successfully established in a considerable business tendered; and because his tender was a few dollars lower than the tender of the man who had operated the route for some time he received the contract. He then turned around and hired someone at less than average wages for that type of work to drive the truck. In my opinion that is one instance of the unfairness of the tender system, and I do not quite know how you are going to overcome it.
In another instance a man took a tender for carrying the rural mail by launch. He had a quite substantial launch. He spent some money in improving it and carried the mail between two or three points some thirty miles apart. Because these isolated communities are served only by a steamer service twice a week he was able to bring in certain supplies required by individuals in the community, and also to carry parcels
Committee on Post Office backward and forward. On several occasions his stout, seaworthy launch-one of the few in the district-was able to take sick people to hospital, and on emergency trips. Somebody else came into the picture and created confusion, against the wishes of all the people concerned in these communities. The matter was discussed for months and months. The man wants to build an even better boat, but he does not know what to do. Even before I came into this house I was interested in community organizations, boards of trade, farmers' institutes, and bodies of that sort; therefore I have a pretty good knowledge of the complexities and difficulties of this problem. In associations that I have been connected with we have often discussed ways and means of

Committee on Post Office correcting various mail situations. I admit again that it is a very difficult problem, but I trust that as a result of a thorough examination of this problem by the committee and with the advice of the officials of the department, when this committee reports its recommendations will make provision for a great improvement in the conditions under which the rural mail is carried in this country.

Mr. Speaker, like those who have spoken before me, I am also in favour of this resolution and only wish that it had been introduced and acted upon many years ago.
The problem of the rural mail courier is one that has taken up quite a little time in the house, and I am glad to see that we have at least secured a minister who has listened to what we members here have to say. I also want to thank him for putting into operation a rural mail route which was put out of business a little while before he came into office, simply because a few dollars were involved. At the present time none too much is being paid.
I believe the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) made a good suggestion when he said to the minister that the expenses of witnesses brought here should be paid, because the expense of coming here might prevent some valuable witnesses from putting in an appearance and giving evidence. We have paid plenty of money by way of expenses to other witnesses, and I hope these expense moneys will not be denied representatives of the rural mail carriers' association.
The system of tendering has been given approval in some places while in other places it has been discredited. If all mail carriers were good businessmen the situation would be somewhat different. However, many of them have been enticed into putting in tenders at figures much below the value of the work involved. The result is that shortly after they begin working they find they are losing money, and on some occasions this results in the giving of poor service. The result is that the people on the route must suffer because of the low tender.
In my home town I know of one carrier, Mr. George Martin, who is on his route six days a week. When I was home at Christmas he suggested something which might be of interest to the committee. He pointed out that some school district buses are paid on a mileage basis. That is, on a paved road the rate is so much per mile, on a gravel road it is slightly different and on a dirt road
[Mr. Herridge.l

another rate is paid. This might be considered with profit by the committee. Then I suggest there should be consideration of the density of population or the number of boxes per mile. This might be helpful to the committee.
I would ask that the committee and the minister give careful consideration to increasing the service from two to three deliveries a week. So far as I know in my constituency we do not receive more than two deliveries a week in any section of the territory which, at the present time, is somewhat in excess of 6,000 square miles. On the other hand people in cities and towns have daily mail service, and we hope provision will be made soon whereby they will have it twice a day.
I think therefore the committee might properly consider giving delivery three days a week in the rural areas. We must remember that the people in the country districts are, in practically all cases, primary producers and, as such, they should have their fair share of the services for which they are paying.
Then there should be some type of security for those people who spend many years of their lives delivering mail over rural routes. Perhaps this would not apply to those who have worked for only a short time; but there are many who have spent the best years of their lives in the delivery of mail, and I suggest the minister might consider making available to them the form of pension given to other members of the post office staff.
I do not wish to take up further time, but I felt I should make these few observations in the hope that they might be of interest to the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I have withheld any remarks I wished to make until this time, when we have before us the motion to set up the special committee. At the outset I should like to say to the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) that, coming from a constituency that has both rural and urban residents about equally divided, I find it necessary to take up many problems with the Post Office Department on behalf of those people. Let me say to you, sir, that I have had the utmost co-operation and success in dealing at the local level with postmasters involved, then with the district inspector, and then with the Postmaster General or his parliamentary assistant, as well as other officers of the department.
When I have discussed with the Postmaster General problems connected with expanding communities in suburban areas, such as were described by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. JANUARY 29, 1953
Graydon), he has been most receptive and, on each occasion, a daily mail delivery service has been put into practise.
Referring now particularly to the rural areas, may I say that I am deeply gratified that finally this matter has reached the point where a committee of the house is to be set up to deal with injustices under the act. One particular amendment that I suggest should be made would be to that section of the act which would seem to prohibit delivery of mail to residents living just off an established route. In bringing this matter to the attention of the minister's officials it has been pointed out to me that it is necessary to have an extension in order to service these people. In my constituency, and I am sure in every constituency across Canada, many who live in rural sections are not receiving regular mail service because of the fact that they are just off a travelled route. While I am not sure, my understanding is that, unfortunately, in order to have an extension of half a mile or a mile in the length of a route it must be established that there are a certain number of boxholders in that district. I have been informed that there most be three to a mile.
Four.

Someone says it is four. I have been confronted with this problem on several occasions. I believe it was the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) who said that we are past the horse and buggy days in the matter of mail delivery, that in these days we do not need to use the horse and buggy or horse and cutter. My only observation would be that a year or so ago I took up residence on a rural route and now receive my domestic mail from a box on that route. I find that, particularly at this time of year, the mail carrier must use a cutter, and that he finds it tough going. In my view he does not receive a bit too much pay for the job.
The hon. member for Victoria, Ont. (Mr. Hodgson) made reference to patronage in his constituency. That may or may not be true. However, it has been pointed out to me that back in the period between 1930 and 1935, when there was another government in office, patronage was rampant not only in the Post Office Department but also in other departments of government.
Name them.

The hon. member asks me to name them. I must admit it was a little before my time. I am talking about something I have been told by members of the opposition. I have found in my dealings 68108-93
Committee on Post Office with the Post Office Department that everything is treated as a straight business proposition and there is no patronage at all. I have been able to secure some redress for those who have contracts under $1,000.
The service required on rural mail routes is increasing all the time. The number of boxholders on practically all routes is increasing. People are moving from the city to the country, and new Canadians are moving into Canada and going to live in areas served by the rural mail routes. The department takes the view in letting contracts that the national average of boxes per mile must be taken into account. That seems to me a wrong principle. On some routes there may be only a few boxholders, while the other routes may cover many boxholders. I think the committee would be well advised to consider such matters as this.
I should like to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General the lack of accommodation in the post office buildings in Belleville and Tweed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to the proposed amendments which are to be studied by the proposed committee, and to conditions which relate to rural mail service.

What I was about to say has some connection with the rural mail carriers. Rural mail carriers operate in all directions from Belleville, and they must sort their mail and take directions from the postmaster there. That applies also to the village of Tweed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member wishes to speak about the condition of distribution centres for rural mail he would be in order.

I should like to point out that the distribution centres are sadly overtaxed. The post office in Belleville was built many years ago to serve rural and urban communities of only a few thousand. Belleville is now a rapidly expanding metropolis with a population large in comparison to what it was when the post office was built. The accommodation has been added to by a little extension to the building here and a little extension to the building there and the putting in of a mezzanine.
The post office at Tweed has become quite active, its revenue being much higher than that of post offices in other villages and towns where new buildings have been erected for the purpose of serving the rural mail carriers. I am pleased that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) is here, and I ask him to consider including an item in the supplementary estimates to cover the construction of new post offices at these two points.

Committee on Post Office
I join with the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) in suggesting that the terms of reference of this committee should be broadened so that it can consider the whole letter carrier situation. I am speaking particularly for the carriers in my area who are members of the federated association of letter carriers. At the present time the remuneration they receive has no relation to the job they are doing. They are expected to be on the job six days a week and carry the mail whether it is snowing and freezing or 90 or 100 degrees in the shade. When compared with the rates received by those in industry we find that the letter carriers are not being treated on a comparative basis.
Letter carriers in the United States receive $4,300 a year as compared with approximately $2,850 received by the letter carriers in this country. I point out further that the letter carriers in the big country to the south work a 40-hour week whereas the letter carriers in Canada must work a 44-hour week. There is some suggestion that the two-a-day mail delivery will be restored. If that is done it will mean that the duties of the letter carriers will be much heavier than they are at the present time. I ask this committee which is to be set up to consider bringing the pay of letter carriers into line. As hon. members know, the letter carriers constitute the public relations department, not only for the government but for parliament as well.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has been referring to letter carriers, which is a considerable distance from rural mail delivery, the subject of the resolution.

I should like to conclude by suggesting to the Postmaster General that this committee consider all phases of the rural mail service and possibly be given an opportunity to look into the wages being paid to our letter carriers.

Mr. Speaker, I have been waiting patiently all afternoon to take a small part in this discussion on rural mail delivery. I want to bring a particular matter to the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) this afternoon because I know he has a special interest in the area which I represent, after having received such a cordial welcome during his visit there last July. I understand it was the first time in a good many years that we had been honoured by a personal visit from the Postmaster General.
I agree in a general way with the remarks of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), but the problem I wish to put before the minister-perhaps we will be able to discuss it later in the committee-is almost the reverse


of the difficulty the hon. member for Peel mentioned. He referred to the problems that have arisen with the development of suburban communities. On the prairies we have the reverse process. As our rural areas have tended to become depopulated and our farms to increase in size, there has been a tendency for some of the rural routes to become uneconomic to operate.
This matter came to my attention quite recently in a specific case when the rural delivery service from the town of Alexander, Manitoba, was abruptly stopped. Apparently the tender submitted for the particular contract was $1,250, but the Post Office Department thought the route could not be operated on an economic basis for more than $1,000.
As I listened to the discussion this afternoon, particularly on the resolution which was before us, it occurred to me that the solution being sought might in some way assist in this problem that is peculiar to the prairies. The matter will have to be considered in the committee; but if the present trend continues and our farm population continues to move towards the cities or suburban areas and as a result farm units become increasingly large, then it may mean that there will have to be further cancellations of service if the situation is only going to be considered on the basis of economic distribution. Such a result of course would not increase the attractiveness of life in rural areas. No doubt the minister is aware of this situation. I think it is of sufficient importance to command the attention of the committee.
I do not know whether I should mention at this time matters pertaining to what have been described as distribution centres, but they are of interest to me. If I can refer to the post office at Brandon as a distribution centre for rural areas, I should like to point out that there has been an appropriation on the books for the past three years-this concerns the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) too-for the expansion of facilities in that city. There has been some considerable delay in carrying out the contemplated program. During the minister's delightful visit to Brandon I think he had a chance to realize the situation, and no doubt the appropriation that has been on the books for three years now will be used in the very near future to correct it.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) on bringing in this motion providing for the setting up of a committee to consider ways and means of assisting rural and urban mail carriers. In my constituency they are practically all rural carriers.

In 1951 I brought in a resolution asking that rural mail carriers receive greater consideration from the Postmaster General. Discussions were carried on with the former postmaster general by myself and other members, and in the session of 1951 legislation was passed making provision for assistance to veterans receiving $1,000 or less. That assistance has proved to be generally quite satisfactory. The committee now being set up will have discussions on ways and means of assisting rural mail carriers now receiving $1,000 or over, and I am quite sure the revision of the legislation that is to be made will be as satisfactory as were the amendments to the Post Office Act of 1951.
As I sat and listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Hastings South (Mr. Foil-well), I fully agreed with what he said about doing away with the present restrictions on the service to rural people who reside on byroads that are not now served by regular rural mail routes. I believe the minimum requirement now stands at four boxholders per mile. In many cases that is working a great hardship on people living off established mail carrier routes. The tendency in rural farming and fishing areas today, especially in farming, is toward larger holdings because the mechanization of farming has brought about the absorption of smaller farm holdings. Therefore the result is that there are fewer residents per mile. When you consider the service the Post Office Department renders to people living in urban areas, who have two and three mail deliveries a day, while on the other hand there are people in rural areas who are not being served at all, or other cases where the woman of the household has to walk two miles to a mailbox, to me it is just not fair. We need these people in the isolated areas. They are producers. I feel quite confident that when this matter comes up for discussion in the committee the Postmaster General will give these people the fullest consideration.

Mr. Speaker, to conform with the very judicious advice given a few moments ago by the chairman, I felt it my duty to refrain from speaking at that time. I trust, however, that I may be permitted to say a few words on the motion to set up a committee.
Previous speakers have spoken at some length about the situation of rural mail couriers, which it is desired to readjust by a method that might be more satisfactory 68108-93i
Committee on Post Office but that could also prove somewhat dangerous for the minister himself, in spite of the fact that he is a man of good will.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) will not deny, I am sure, that, as a rule, rural mail couriers are not sufficiently paid for the work they perform. It is easy to say that they themselves set their own price. However, because they are free to quote a price according to their own judgment, things are not always as simple as that.
What usually happens is that someone in the postal district where tenders are called decides to send in his own tender. He has learned somehow or other what was the amount of the contract of the previous mail courier. Once his contract is secured, he soon realizes that the scope of his responsibilities is much more extensive than he first imagined. His plight becomes unbearable. He makes this situation known to his member who, I imagine, passes his request on to the minister with the grievances of the man concerned. During the period which preceded the nomination of the present minister, as far as I know, the minister used to answer invariably, "Very well, if the holder of the contract is not satisfied, let him drop his contract and it will be up to him to put in a new tender". That was not a solution to the problem. Let us hope that the procedure for obtaining a contract under the bill, which has just been read for the first time, brings about a practical solution to this problem.
I would like to add only a few words in connection with another aspect of this question, which I will no doubt be able to discuss since the committee we are being requested to form will no doubt be able to look into the operation of rural mail services.
I am thinking now of the extension of rural mail service to rather distant parts of some concessions. In these concessions are sometimes to be found two, three or four farmers who do not enjoy rural mail delivery and who are therefore in a very difficult position indeed.
I understand that the minister is bound by the present regulations and that he can do no more, in spite of his good intentions. Unless I am mistaken there must be at least four or five residents over a one-mile stretch before these people become entitled to rural mail delivery. The farmers, moreover, it must be remembered, do not enjoy the privilege of going to the post office on Sundays since these are now closed. Formerly they were

Committee on Post Office open before or after high mass, sometimes in the afternoon and certainly in the evening, so that these people could be sure of meeting there to transact their postal business and many other things. But this is all over now. On the other hand the farmers do not have as many occasions of going down to the village as they had in former days. They generally sell their produce on their own doorstep and the things they buy are generally delivered there too. So that they must make a special trip of four, five or six miles to post a letter or get their mail, which they now receive quite frequently, for today our farmers read the daily newspapers.
For these reasons, I think that the rural mail service should be extended, that there should be a means of making a thorough survey of the situation, precisely during the proceedings of a committee such as the one we propose to establish. There should be a means of correcting this anomaly so that the farmers, even those who live in remote areas, may receive their mail if not every day at least every second day.
You will allow me here to quote a fact. A group of four farmers have established themselves on the land of their forefathers on land which had been opened up a few generations ago. Now one of these farmers sold his land and settled elsewhere for the one and only reason that he had no access to a daily postal service.
I trust that, knowing the minister's good -will, it will be possible, when this matter is studied in committee, to correct this situation.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is a matter of very great satisfaction to all members of parliament and to all parties in the house that the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) has finally acceded to the oft-repeated request made not only by members of the opposition but by other parties as well to discuss this matter in detail, particularly as it applies to the general administration of rural mail delivery and the problems of the couriers. I think this is the first time a real attempt has been made to deal with this matter, which has never been given the attention and consideration that it should have received. It involves a group of people that have served this country and the postal department very ably.
I think I express the views of members who have a knowledge of the responsibility, the work and all that is involved when a rural mail contract is signed. When we think of the thousands of people who day by day loyally carry Her Majesty's mail during

winter and summer, through sunshine and storm, we realize that these people feel that above all the mail must go through. We must consider that in carrying out their duties these people handle millions of dollars worth of securities and papers. We also must associate with them, Mr. Speaker, those who serve urban municipalities in a like capacity. We find that there have been very, very few cases where mishandling or misappropriation of funds has been charged against those people. I think it is very commendable that such is the case.
There are no horses in the mail bags.

I think it has been proved that these people have been honest and loyal in carrying out their duties.
As was mentioned by the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White), the post office does serve all the people of Canada, regardless of whether we are rich or poor, regardless of our station in life; we are all treated alike in the service we get from the rural mail couriers.
I trust that the committee will go into all aspects of the work very thoroughly, and deal not only with the service of the couriers but with the other services which can be rendered by this department.
I hope serious study will be given to the possibility of bringing in a recommendation that rural mail couriers should come under some form of civil service provision. That may not be possible, but every member of parliament who represents a rural constituency knows of individual cases where these men have been carrying the mail ten, twenty and thirty years or even more but are not in a position today to even buy a late model car with which to carry out their duties. I think it is an indication that, as we all agree, these men are not receiving sufficient remuneration. It does seem to me that for service in this field some more permanent policy should be put into effect to at least in part compensate them for their years of work. A system might be inaugurated whereby after five years of proven service a pension plan would be open to them. A general scheme might be worked out uniformly on a mileage basis with due consideration being given to conditions in the locality or municipality.
If we could eliminate the tender system that is presently in effect I think we would be taking a step which would greatly advance the situation, considering all the responsibilities and the duties which mail couriers are called upon to perform.
There are many other details which I hope and trust will be gone into very carefully

by the committee which has been set up for the purpose. We realize that the problems are most perplexing and most difficult. They will not be solved too easily. This committee have a big job to do, and they will be required to undertake a full analysis of the many factors which will arise during their deliberations.
I cannot help but feel that this legislation is a step forward, and I hope it will at least partially solve the situation that should have been faced years and years ago. I trust also that it will eliminate the unfavourable factors that have been associated with the Post Office Department, in connection with political aspects which in many cases have not been conducive to what we consider good and above-board principles.
I would like to emphasize the statement made by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) when he said that every facility should be extended to these people in order that they may come and give evidence which will assist the Postmaster General and the committee. Knowing the Postmaster General as we do, I am sure he will give them a favourable reception and that after their suggestions are heard action will be taken. As a result, Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in supporting a recommendation to set up this committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad of the opportunity this resolution gives to say a few words with regard to matters concerning mail deliveries in the rural areas.
I am quite sure everyone in the house has had the same experience I have had, that when we take these matters up with the Postmaster General, particularly the present incumbent of the office, we receive pleasant, courteous and agreeable replies to our representations. They always appear to be approached in a sympathetic manner. I think it is correct to say-at any rate it is my own experience-that we are encouraged by these replies to hope that at last we have found a really sympathetic Postmaster General and that we are going to have all our requests accepted.
But unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the realization does not always measure up to the anticipation which this extremely pleasant attitude has aroused. If therefore I am somewhat critical this afternoon of affairs with respect to the rural services, I hope the Postmaster General will not take it amiss but will realize that I am sincere when I say that we appreciate his courtesy, that we are quite ready to believe that the lack of universal success in getting our requests accepted is probably not his fault, that if it were left
Committee on Post Office to him alone we would get them all, but that he is not able to do all he would like to do for us.
Nevertheless, that does not alter the fact that-in my experience, at any rate, in my constituency-the service to rural areas is far from improving to the extent which I believe it should improve, particularly when viewed in relation to the improvements in service and the speed of service in the more settled districts, but has in fact followed a retrograde course.
I have before me notes and correspondence that I have been having with the Postmaster General concerning five rural mail problems in my constituency. In the first of these there has been a reduction in the service. The second one is an effort to restore a service which was taken away twenty years ago. In the third one there has been a complete elimination of a service in existence for thirty years. In the fourth one, as the result of an alteration made in the general set-up of one service, there has been the elimination of another service, this time after forty years. And in the fifth one there is the threat of the elimination of a rural service. This state of affairs is spread throughout the whole constituency; it is not just in one area. You can therefore see, Mr. Speaker, that there is cause for concern and complaint on the part of the residents of the rural districts of my constituency with respect to the mail service which they are receiving.
I want to take this opportunity of impressing upon the minister the need of the people of these particular districts for a restored or an improved service. I have in mind, first, the matter of mail service to Beaton, which lies at the head of the Arrow lakes. It is served by a ferry boat which runs three times a week between Arrowhead and Beaton. There used to be a thrice-weekly mail service. That service has been reduced in recent months from three times a week to twice a week; and that reduction, may I say, Mr. Speaker, has taken place in the face of the fact that there is a great increase in the mining activity in that area.
I have had letters from the chamber of commerce in the district and from others concerned in the mining business, and they have impressed upon me the great inconvenience that reduction causes. I passed this information and these requests on to the Post Office Department, and as I say, we have had sympathetic letters; but so far, unfortunately, although a review has been promised, we have had no results. I want therefore to take this opportunity of laying before the Postmaster General the case of this service which at the moment is being investigated
1456	HOUSE OF
Committee on Post Office by his inspector in Vancouver, and to ask him if he will give it his own personal attention and give the necessary instructions that the service be restored from twice a week to three times a week.
The next area is at a place called Chezacut. It is in the district known as the Chilcotin, one of the finest ranching areas in the province. It is an area which lies well beyond the limits of ordinary settlement. I am not going to say that it lies beyond the limits of civilization, because that would be going too far; but in so far as we have a frontier area left in our part of the country, it is a frontier area. The people living at this point are some sixty miles from the nearest post office. I am informed that up until 1933 there was a regular service between Redstone and Chezacut. That service was discontinued in 1933. The result is that there are several families, with at least 25 children-that was the information I received in 1950-
Individual families?
There are several families, and a total of 25 children.
That is better than the Frenchmen.

It is a virile country. These families and children are without mail service. When I wrote the Postmaster General about this matter, again I received a letter which promised an immediate investigation; but unfortunately the investigation resulted in a report which informed me that the Postmaster General decided it would not be possible to restore this mail service. The reason he gave us was that on account of the mileage that it would be necessary to cover and the fact that there were not very many families in the district, the result would be-and I quote from his letter-that "we would show a considerable deficit as the cost of this service would be far in excess of the expected revenue".
I do not want to get into a discussion of general principles here-I will do that in a moment or two-but I just want to pause to suggest that when you are considering services to rural areas, it is not proper to place the matter exclusively on a financial basis and say that unless the service will show a profit or at least will not operate at a deficit, we will not give the service; because that attitude results in a situation which makes it almost impossible for families to live in those districts, particularly families with children where it is necessary sometimes to get word out in a hurry, in the case of emergencies, or where it is necessary to carry on correspondence courses for education. The people


simply cannot get their children educated; they cannot bring them up with the amenities and facilities they should have, when most services are denied as a result of erroneous insistence on the necessity of showing an operating profit before inaugurating or continuing rural mail service.
The third case concerns Heffley Creek rural route No. 2, which is another case in which the service has been discontinued. This service was in existence continuously for some thirty years until it was cut off this summer. By constituents there, I am advised that the service was "cut off abruptly this month"- that is the month of July

"with just a note in the mailbox stating it was to be the last delivery". My correspondent goes on to say that he has four children who depend on the mail delivery for their correspondence lessons. Well, I took this matter up with the Postmaster General, and as a result of these inquiries I received a rather unusual letter from him in which he gave as the main reason for the discontinuance of the route the fact that the road conditions were poor, on account of which the courier had asked for an increase in the amount of his contract. He previously operated it for $364 per annum, $7 per trip. When the contract expired a renewal was offered, but he refused it and submitted another tender at the rate of $600 per annum, which he subsequently agreed to reduce to $550, and the department felt that that was too high. They went on to say that one of the reasons given for the rate, according to the tenderer, was the deplorable condition of the road which the tenderer said resulted in large bills for the repair and maintenance of his car.
The Postmaster General went on to say that the residents who wanted the route continued should improve their road if they really wanted a rural route. The Postmaster General does not appear to appreciate the conditions. What he is doing is to require the people, who live there as individuals, to maintain some thirty miles of road, which is of course entirely a provincial responsibility.
In British Columbia there is no longer the system of the old days-and it had its advantages-whereby the farmers living in the country areas had the opportunity of working out their taxes by doing a certain amount of road work. That system has not been followed for some time by our provincial administration, and there is no way in which the farmers, who are busy enough as it is at any rate, can keep up the road.
This seems to me to be another case in which the department just does not recognize

the difficulties under which the inhabitants of those rural areas are living. The fact that the road conditions are poor and the conditions of life are strenuous is, I submit, an additional reason why every effort should be made by all governmental authorities to do what they can to bring to the people the amenities which will make their life a little less hard, and generally make conditions under which they live a little more pleasant. Certainly the regular receipt of mail is one of the things to which people in rural areas most look forward. Here we have a condition where instead of their circumstances being improved, and everything possible to improve them being done, they are compelled to accept a worse state of affairs as the years go by, and the service which they enjoyed for thirty years has now been discontinued.
The fourth case concerns the mail service in the Ashcroft-Clinton area, the gateway to the Cariboo ranching country. Here a mail service which was in operation for forty years has been discontinued. This state of affairs came about as the result of a change in the mail service on the Cariboo highway. We had been pressing for a matter of some five years for a daily service to the main post offices on the Cariboo highway, from Ashcroft north. On September 15 last, after these lengthy negotiations, the department suddenly announced its decision to implement this service. I might say that they announced it by means of informing the residents in the Clinton area that they would no longer be receiving their thrice weekly service which they had received by a rural courier. That was the first indication that they or I or anyone else had that the decision had been arrived at to institute this daily service, by bus from Ashcroft, to the main post offices on the Cariboo highway.
The reason given for the discontinuance of this rural service is that the department will not maintain two parallel services, one a rural service to the boxes along the highway, while at the same time there is what you might call a main line service from Ashcroft, dropping off mails to the main post offices along the same route.
Well, it may be difficult to argue against that, at least in theory, but there are two observations I should like to make. The first is that I do not think it was proper that this decision should be made and implemented without any warning to anyone concerned that the result of the change-that is the institution of the daily service by bus to the main post offices-would be the discontinuance of another service. That fact had simply not been discussed. Secondly, it
Committee on Post Office means that all the other rural points dependent on service from Clinton as their central post office have had their mail service changed as well, because the decision to institute the daily main post office service covers only first-class letter mail. Previously, in the area from Ashcroft to Clinton, there was the three times a week service, and in other cases once a week rural service, which carried all classes of mail, parcels as well as letters. That has been discontinued, and parcels have to go by train, with long delays, and letters only are carried by the daily service to Clinton. One of the rural services has been discontinued as a result, and with respect to the other services they receive only letters; they have to wait a very much longer time before they get their parcels.
A petition has been submitted to the Postmaster General asking that this matter be taken care of by providing that the daily service to the main post offices, which would include Clinton, should carry all classes of mail, and that a separate rural service be instituted covering the points between Ashcroft and Clinton formerly served three times a week. Whatever the method adopted, Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that the result of the change has been that a service to a rural area which contains a very large number of people, which had been in existence for forty years with reasonable satisfaction, has suddenly been discontinued.
I sent a petition to the minister covering one portion of this area, asking for the reinstitution of the rural route. I have received the usual courteous answer, but so far have had no action. Sometimes it seems to me that it takes the minister's department a very long time to get their reports, because it is well over six weeks since the matter was referred to him. A report was promised, but I have had no further word.
The final case I want to bring to the minister's attention concerns rural route No. 1 at Pritchard. Here again is a case of a route which has been in existence for many years, now threatened with discontinuance because the contractor finds it impossible to continue operating at the present rate. I must say that the residents of that route appreciate the fact that a temporary authorization was granted for the continuance of the route at a higher rate, but that arrangement is not permanent. It is merely continued at the Postmaster General's pleasure, and might be cancelled at any time. What we want there is authority for the contract at a rate which will enable a tenderer living in the area to operate without loss. Just because the costs of operation have increased-the population has not gone

Committee on Post Office down; in fact it has increased somewhat-is, I submit, no justification for discontinuing a service which is essential to those who live there. A contract must be awarded at a rate which will enable the carrier to operate with safety and certainty.
Mr. Speaker, these are five problems which concern the residents of rural areas in my constituency, so far as their mail service is concerned. I submit that each one of these could be satisfactorily settled by the application of the general principle which I maintain should apply, namely that those living in the rural areas of Canada are now entitled to priority in the matter of their mail service.
After all, the cities and urban areas in Canada would not exist if it were not for the rural areas lying behind them. If it were not for the produce of the farms, the forests and the mines of Canada we would not have any cities, because there would be no justification or occasion for them. Yet rural areas in most cases have inadequate service and exist under conditions of great hardship. Now they are beginning to find their conditions made even worse because, at least in those cases I have outlined, they have been deprived even of those meagre mail services they formerly had.
Keep in mind that city life has all the amenities. People in the cities do not have to expose themselves to an equal extent to the rigours of winter. They have all conveniences right at their doorstep. They have the advantage of mail delivery and parcel post, regular deliveries from the shops, and the like. They do not have to drive through snowdrifts on rough country roads to obtain the very necessities of life. Yet these cities, already enjoying an adequate mail delivery service, suddenly found themselves, a year or two ago, in receipt of the de luxe all-up air mail service, a service provided only at the expense of the whole country which of course includes the rural areas. I have not been able this afternoon to find the figure among my papers, but I recall that I did receive from the Postmaster General figures showing the increase in cost to the Post Office Department as the result of this all-up air mail service.
I am not suggesting that this service should be eliminated. But I do suggest that if it is to be given at the general expense of the country, including the taxpayers in rural areas; if our cities are to be given this super de luxe service when already they were enjoying a quite adequate service, then surely the rural areas should be provided with an adequate service instead of the


meagre and, in some cases, totally inadequate service from which they have been suffering for so many years.
This argument of course has double application to cases such as I have outlined this afternoon, where an already meagre service is either going to be discontinued, or made more inadequate through having the deliveries reduced from three to two each week.
I repeat that if the cities of Canada can be given this super service at the general expense of the taxpayers, including those in the rural areas, upon whom the cities depend, then it is time-more than time-that adequate service be provided for those who live in the rural areas, without whose willingness to endure hardships and to go to the country and produce the things we all require there could be no existence for those of us who live in the cities.
I am sure if this problem were put to any individual living in a city he would say, "Surely; I agree with you. Let us give the farmers, the ranchers, those working in the mines and the forests an adequate service." Let us cut out this penny-pinching which results in destroying in some cases even the amenities of mail service they already had, and let us get on with improving rural service generally.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw to the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) and the committee which is to be set up under this motion a condition under which the rural patrons of the post office do not receive the same consideration as city patrons. This motion is to set up a committee to investigate the regulations and the general administration and operation of rural mail delivery services, and I feel that this is a proper place to call the attention of the Postmaster General to the anomaly which I will now describe.
When first-class mail is posted in a post office it is delivered for three cents when it can be handled through that post office. But in the case of a rural post office, where there are no walks by letter carriers, a letter to be called for at that particular office or deliv-

ered by a rural mail courier must have a four-cent stamp placed upon it. I feel that that is a discrimination against the rural patrons of the Post Office Department. The principle is that if a letter passes through one office only it is delivered for three cents irrespective of the method of delivery. In the cities it is delivered by letter carriers performing their usual walks; in the country districts it is delivered by rural mail carriers using a car or a horse and buggy in order to deliver mail to the patrons of that particular post office.
This works a particular hardship upon that large class of patrons who live in what was described by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) as suburbia, that borderland between rural and urban communities. Let me give an example of a condition which exists throughout the dominion, and I use the city of Victoria, British Columbia, as my example.
A letter posted in the post office there to be delivered to 2000 Quadra street will be delivered by a letter carrier on his walk for three cents. But if it is addressed to 2100 Quadra street it will be delivered by a rural mail carrier and must bear a four-cent stamp. The line which is taken as the limit of three-cent postage does not conform at all to the city boundary, it is an arbitrary line which was drawn a number of years ago by the Post Office Department. It was suitable in those days, but the environs of the city of Victoria have built up tremendously, and unless one had a map with that particular line drawn upon it he would not know when he passed from the three-cent to the four-cent area.
One of the main difficulties is that a business or professional man living just over the border must pay additional postage due every time he receives any mail with a three-cent stamp upon it. Many of the city streets run through this imaginary line. A correspondent addressing a letter might consult the city or telephone directory to find an address; and if the address was 2000 Quadra street his letter would be delivered for three cents. But another person looking up another address and finding it to be 2100 Quadra street would make it necessary for the professional or businessman who might be living at that number to pay extra postage due if only three cents were placed upon the letter.
I am using this just as an illustration. I am not suggesting for one moment that 2100 is actually the number of a house on that particular street. This is the condition that exists in Victoria, and I think a similar condition exists in every rural post office 68108-94
Committee on Post Office throughout the land. If you deliver a letter at a rural post office, unless it is to be called for at the post office it can be delivered only by a rural mail carrier. Although it goes through only the one office it must have a four-cent stamp on it. Surely the principle is that if a letter is posted in one office to be delivered to a person through that office it should require only three cents. If it is to go through two offices, naturally there should be a four-cent stamp upon it.
Surely the matter of delivery is not of prime concern. If it is possible to deliver a letter for three cents through one city post office to addresses in that city, that letter being delivered by hand at the door to the person to whom it is addressed, surely the same privilege should be granted to the rural patrons of the post office. When they receive a letter which only goes through one office it should be possible to carry it to them for three cents, no matter what the method of delivery is.
I would therefore ask the Postmaster General to give this matter his consideration, because there is an anomaly there. There is great difficulty with the borderline cases where the Post Office Department has drawn an arbitrary line between letter carrier delivery and rural courier delivery. A person writing a letter cannot tell where that line is, and it is a hardship on the residents of the kind of area which was described as suburbia today by the hon. member for Peel.
These people are very definitely handicapped because they have to pay the amount of the postage due stamps, and in the case of business and professional men it sometimes amounts to quite a large sum. I cannot help feeling that it is only fair that rural patrons who receive their mail through one office should not be required to pay more for the delivery of their mail through that one office than a city resident has to pay for the delivery of his mail through one office. I hope the Postmaster General will give the matter very careful consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief. I want to speak on behalf of the rural carriers in my riding. I am not worried, as was the previous speaker, about whether my pre-election speeches will be delivered at any particular rate. It is rather amazing to me that a member coming from a district adjacent to Victoria would want anything delivered except an obituary notice, which would be customary in the city of Victoria.
I do want to say that I think the system is wrong under which rural carriers are operating at the present time. I do not know

Committee on Post Office what the solution is, but I believe a committee of the house might consider the matter and arrive at some decision satisfactory both to the public and to the carriers. Unlike my friend from Nanaimo, I am not worrying about whether it costs three or four cents to send my speeches to my constituents because I would prefer, as I think he should, that they do not get there.
I think the present system is not good for the public or the carriers. I know that in my own riding people have bid for carrier routes at rates at which they could not carry out their contracts profitably. I think they bid on them knowing that they could not be carried out at the rates at which they tendered. What the solution is I frankly admit I do not know; and I am perfectly sure that the hon. member for Nanaimo, with all his vast carrier experience, both pigeon and otherwise, does not know the solution. However, I believe the matter could be referred to a committee.
I want to say that I think the present system on the contract basis is entirely wrong, and that a committee should be set up to study it.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take very much of the time of the house because this subject has been thoroughly discussed. Neither do I wish to embarrass the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote), but may I say that I agree with the many kind things that were said about him this afternoon. I am sure that his genial manner and pleasant smile are going to help him a lot in his portfolio. I also feel he is not likely to fall into some of the errors that his predecessor committed.
I am pleased that a committee is to be set up. Such action has been recommended before in the house, and I think a committee can do a lot of good. People from all parts of Canada will come before the committee to express their views on this most difficult problem, and I know that good results will attend the work of the committee.
There are many problems, and having listened to the members who spoke this afternoon one realizes that the problems are the same in practically every constituency, particularly the rural ones. My own constituency is about 80 per cent rural, and I think it has as many rural mail routes as any other constituency in Canada. The great problem in the past has been the difficulty of the courier in obtaining suitable compensation for the work he was doing. I think this situation has been brought about by the keen competition for these jobs. Why there should be such

keen competition is hard for me to understand because, as has been pointed out here, it is a very difficult and important job, and the mail couriers certainly have to cope with the weather and many other difficulties.
I agree with what was said this afternoon by a number of members from rural constituencies about people in the rural districts not receiving the same treatment as those in the cities. To my mind there is no reason in the world why a city district should have two daily mail deliveries whereas in some country districts they only have three mail deliveries a week. I think that is most unfair, and as long as that situation prevails there is going to be a great deal of dissatisfaction throughout the country. I also believe that, while the present system of obtaining mail couriers is obsolete and unsatisfactory, we must be very careful not to institute a system which will be on a patronage basis. I think such action would lead to much difficulty and abuse. When the committee meets I am sure it will give this matter very serious consideration.
I should also like to point out to the minister with respect to rural mail delivery that I believe one of the reasons a good many people are leaving the country districts today, especially the back country areas, is the fact that they are not receiving sufficient mail service. People in the cities have their radios and now their television sets, and they have two daily mail deliveries; but people in the back areas are only getting mail two or three times a week. They cannot have their daily papers and this all works great hardship on them.
I am not going to worry the house this evening with the many problems I have in my own constituency. There will be opportunity to do that later. I have already brought many of them to the attention of the department and some have been corrected, while others have not. I would like, however, to read to the house a typical letter which I received some time ago which illustrates, I think, the problem there is in the country. This has to do with .... rural route No. 2. The writer says:
We have had no mail driver on this route for the past four months. Our mail driver gave up the route because it did not pay him. I understand that a tender went in, approved by the local executive, but that Ottawa would not contract. I presume that the authorities figure it on a mileage basis but it is more than that.
The driver leaves at ten a.m. in order to have
the mail at	 by eleven o'clock. Then he
has to wait for two trains and the sorting of the mail, getting home about five p.m. Thus, it takes his whole day for a thirty-mile trip.
That is an indication, Mr. Speaker-and there are many-why you cannot stick to

any hard and fast rule as far as mileage is concerned. This man spends his whole day and he should be entitled, as I am sure the minister will agree, to a full day's pay. The result in that district was that they could not get a man to drive the mail on the basis that is now in effect. The writer goes on to say:
I believe we have a right to the same service that we are helping to pay for in the rest of Canada and ask that you advise us at your earliest convenience what we are to expect for we have been slighted too long.
That is just an indication of the feeling of many people in many sections, not only of my own province but I am sure all across Canada.
As I said at the outset I am certainly well pleased that the minister is setting up this committee, and I believe these many problems will need to be carefully considered. I also feel certain that some solution can be found.

Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of points that I would like to bring to the attention of the minister with respect to our particular part of Canada. One of them has to do with air service. I think you should use aircraft more than you do now in servicing these rural routes. An aircraft based at the international airport in Vancouver, running due north through the Cariboo, I am prepared to say, could on a daily run carry all the mail more cheaply than it is being carried today, shuffling it over the railways, back to Edmonton, up and down the P.G.E., the C.P.R., the C.N.R and the other railways, carrying mail clerks and adding unnecessarily to the cost of getting mail over the rural routes. I hope you will study that suggestion and either make contracts or put on your own mail plane from the international airport at Vancouver to say Whitehorse and back, on a daily schedule, so the mail may be delivered promptly and smartly from the central office to those industrial districts along that route.
I think the minister might well consider establishing a base rate for all road transportation of mail. The public utilities commission in British Columbia will establish the cost of hauling goods from one point to another, at so many cents per ton mile. For motor transportation it could be accurately established and it might very well be considered, when calling for tenders, whether the department could say that the base rate would be so many cents per ton mile. From there on it would be a matter of efficiency and people could compete in any way they liked, but we should not send the mail at less than the actual cost to the man doing the work.

Up in our district it is difficult to get couriers to carry the mail from the central office out into the country. They are throwing up their contracts because they do not want to work for nothing. After all, the cost of gasoline, tires and so on is standardized. Everybody knows what they cost. Even hourly labour rates are well standardized. The department could say that in a certain area the base price would be so much. If the work could be done for that, all right; if not, more would have to be paid.
As I say, a good many of those people delivering mail in my area are doing so just out of a sense of duty and service. They are losing money on every load they carry. In that connection I would say that the British Yukon Navigation Company is carrying mail on the Alaska highway from railhead to points in the Yukon at very much less than the actual outlay they are forced to make in order to carry that mail. They are doing that as a service to people along the way.
The government of Canada should not depend upon charity. We should pay these men a fair sum for the work done, and it can be reckoned very easily these days when costs are so well known.
I want to commend the department for the good work which they are doing. I think the minister is following in the footsteps of that great Liberal, Sir William Mulock, who introduced penny postage and who was such an ornament in this house and such a figure in world history when he occupied the position which is now so honourably occupied by the minister.	,

Mr. Speaker, a good many members have entered this debate, and it has now become a wide open debate on postal matters. I suppose we can deal with pretty nearly any part of the Postmaster General's department which may have come to our attention.
The resolution to set up a committee to deal with postal courier matters and other things in connection with the postal department is one for which we on this side of the house have agitated for a number of years. Now we have the support of both sides of the house, and we have the assurance of the Postmaster General that he is in favour of this committee which, particularly, will study rural mail couriers to see that those men, who are great servants of Canada, get what is fair and just treatment.
We all know what the mail couriers have gone through in the years of service which some of them have given. We all know how niggardly they have been treated with regard to salary, but they have not been niggardly

Committee on Post Office in the time they worked, in order to make even their small salaries. We know that no other class of servants of the government has given such service as have these mail couriers who are now being given consideration by this house.
