I just thought that possibly it would be well, Mr. Speaker, to remind the house that I had not forgotten the promises that have been made for ten years or more. That is all I shall say about this dangling of the new post office building.
There are several things I want to speak about tonight and bring to the attention of the new Postmaster General. One is the manner in which we have been treated as a postal area in connection with mail couriers. As a postal area, the province of Prince Edward Island has not had the attention it should have had. For instance, we do not have a divisional controller, nor do we have a postal zone like Nova Scotia or New Brunswick. Instead of having a postal area and a post office division of our own, we are hitched on to the province of New Brunswick. We have the same set-up, nevertheless we have no control, as it were, of our wants.
At the post office at Charlottetown we have some of the best postmasters and inspectors, and the whole staff are excellent as I know the Postmaster General will find out if he has not already done so. We have an excellent staff there. Yet if some rural post offices want some little item in order to complete their rural post office work, they come in and, instead of being able to get it right there in Charlottetown, they have no say in the matter. The first thing they say is: We have to find out from Saint John, New Brunswick. They write or telephone to Saint John and the Saint John man says:	No; there is
the controller at Moncton to whom I have to go. So they go again from Charlottetown to Saint John, then from Saint John to Moncton, and then the Moncton controller has got to go back to Ottawa. Probably by that time


they have forgotten all about what they needed, and nothing more is heard about it until another person comes in.
The usual runaround.

I mention this matter because we, as a province, should have the same treatment as the other provinces receive. We should have control of our own postal affairs. We have been neglected in this matter. It seems to me that the Liberal party, knowingly or otherwise, like to take these things away from our province, if they can possibly do so, in order to make it smaller.
I want to call to the attention of the Postmaster General the fact that his predecessor went one better than that when he was advertising postal matters all across Canada and in the United States. What did he do but get out a map of Canada and leave Prince Edward Island off the map altogether. All hon. members will remember that incident. It cost a great deal of money to rectify that error, because the contracts had been made and the government had to cancel the contracts and pay for them without getting the advertising.
I now want to deal for a few minutes with another little matter that I desire to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General, namely the stamp vendor's position in the post office at Prince Edward Island. There is a stamp vendor there who has been employed by the government for a number of years.

I would take it, Mr. Speaker, that we are to confine ourselves more to the rural mail couriers, and that we can elaborate possibly a little bit more on that matter. However, I think at some stage during this debate there should be a time when we would be able to bring forward certain matters that are worrying us, more or less, with regard to the postal department.

A few moments ago I was speaking about the mail couriers and saying what a wonderful class of citizens they are. I am dealing more particularly with the constituency of Queens. In that constituency the great trouble we have always had with reference to mail couriers' contracts has been the great discrepancy between the various mail routes. No matter how much alike they were, in the granting of contracts these differences came into the picture. As an illustration, let us consider contracts for routes covering only eight miles. They were only small contracts, yet in those contracts there was a difference of as much as $120 a year. That was on an eight-mile contract. Then we come along to the nine and ten-mile contracts. Here the discrepancy goes up according to the people who have the job of driving the mail. The discrepancy goes up to $210 on a distance of ten miles, with the lowest-paid courier serving 50 per cent more boxes than were served by any two of the others put together. Yet he is paid $210 a year less.
I want the Postmaster General to remember some of these things when this committee is set up; and I want him to see that the committee endeavours to get as fair a remuneration as it is possible to get for each mail route. Now we come to the twelve and thirteen-mile contracts. Under this system that we have there is a difference of $250 on a considerable number of contracts. Surely there should not be that much difference.
Committee on Post Office On a fourteen-mile route we have a difference of $320 per annum on a small contract of $900.
These discriminations between the different contracts and contractors run as high as $650. These contractors give practically the same service. Some of them work on highways on which they can use automobiles possibly ten months in a year. I hope the committee will take that into consideration. Some of the contractors I have mentioned must have not only a small truck to deliver mail in the summer time, but in the spring they must have a horse and buggy, or a horse and wagon, and in the winter time they must have a horse and cutter. Therefore they all have a certain amount of expense. When the expenses of most of the couriers are calculated, together with the cost of everything they have to buy, such as feed for the horse, horseshoeing, harness repairs of different kinds, as well as the expense of an automobile, and so forth, very few of them make a decent daily wage.
Why are we limited in what we may say in regard to these contractors when we are discussing this new legislation that has been sought and is to be introduced, that will put into the hands of the Postmaster General the right to bargain with the mail couriers on all contracts under a thousand dollars, and some over that amount as well? This is giving too much power to one man. No matter how good a man he may be, power is being put into his hands to enable him to work in the interests of the party to which he belongs. He cannot help but take into account the interests of his own people when it comes to making mail contracts.	j
I am not going to labour this question any longer. There are many things I should like to say but I will abide by your decision, Mr. Speaker. I hope that later on the Speaker will permit me to say what I have to say to the Postmaster General. I now want to give him a word of advice. We had a Postmaster General not so long ago who on several occasions promised us that a committee would be set up, but it was never done. We now have an hon. gentleman who in his first speech to this house as Postmaster General told us that he was going to have it set up. He is therefore in right with all the people across this country who favour working in the interests of the mail couriers.
I have one further word to say to him. I should like to see him cut clear entirely from politics because my memory of his predecessor amuses me, especially in connection with his political career. He has been promoted to something higher, and we have

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to prolong the debate, but as I am not on the committee-and I am not blaming anyone for that-I would like to make a few suggestions now.
First, when the time comes to award contracts, we often receive representations, especially when the said contracts concern two adjacent territories, because there is a discrepancy of $200 or $300. It sometimes happens that people put in such or such a bid because the roads are bad during the winter. Quite often, also, the rural mail courier has to beat his own way in the morning after a storm; that is not very interesting. That man must have a better horse or better equipment. That is why the amount of his tender is a little higher.
Secondly, sometimes there is a request for a box at the end of a road and the minister replies that the distance is too great between the last box on the route and the one asked for. Therefore, I would ask that the distance prescribed be increased because the man who happens to live too far from the last box to be able to get one himself seems to be somewhat neglected, and although he might have the best disposition in the world, he feels inclined to criticize the department; however we do not want this to happen because the department does its best to please everybody.
Thirdly, when there is a request for sorting frames used in preparing the mail to be delivered the next day, it seems only fair to me that those sorting frames be sent to the post office as soon as possible, so as to make things easier for the couriers and enable them to do a good job.
Fourthly, we would ask the public-and we have the right to do so-to co-operate with the rural couriers so that, in winter, when the snow piles up, the latter are not obliged to shovel a path to the owner's mail box. As often happens, even if the courier asks the owner to clear his walk, the owner does not bother to do so. We would like the department to ask the general public to make the work of the rural mail courier somewhat easier since the latter is deserving of much attention and much praise for the way in which he goes about his business.
Now, again, there is the matter of one mail route in one parish encroaching upon another parish. For instance, there are people in Les Ecureuils who have to have their mail addressed to Neuville since they are served


by the Neuville courier, whose circuit extends to the parish of Les Ecureuils. It seems to me there should be a way of preventing the rural mail route of a parish from extending into the neighbouring parish, and even more so when a route passes from one constituency to another.
These are the only remarks I wished to make, Mr. Speaker. I hope that I have not taken too much of the time of the house and that the minister will forgive me for having detained him for a few minutes.

Mr. Speaker, there are three things I want to say. I have found that the salaries paid to those who work in rural post offices are very low, amounting to $13 and $15 a month. We know that an expert woodcutter, cutting wood in the bush, can earn more in a day than would run those post offices for a month. We do not think they get enough.
The second thing I notice is that this is legislation to amend the Post Office Act so that we shall have deliveries twice a day. I will not push that very far, but we need that in the cities and the Postmaster General knows it.
As I mentioned this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I think this way of choosing civil servants by contract has become obsolete. Why cannot these men or women be chosen in the same way as other civil servants are chosen? They have responsible jobs. Why can they not be chosen by examination? I hope this suggestion will be considered.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take much time in the discussion of this motion. I find myself deeply interested in it, and it is one with which I can say I agree.
I could spend some time in bringing to the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) problems of my own constituency, just as other members might do. Thus far my contact with the Postmaster General has been most pleasant indeed. I am sure no one could have extended greater courtesy to me. I have not bothered him much because not long ago he told me legislation would be brought down which he hoped would meet many of the problems not only in my constituency but across Canada as a whole.
I believe this motion to set up the committee is a move in the right direction, provided the members of the committee really get down to business and make an effort to find a method for the proper appointment and payment of rural mail couriers. This

is not going to be an easy matter, because I suppose that conditions vary throughout the country. Different conditions will be found in different constituencies. Perhaps it will not simply be a matter of setting down a basic rate per mile.
In my own constituency, for instance, in the summer the rural mail courier can carry out his task without any great difficulty. But in the winter time he faces an entirely different situation, and it is not unreasonable that, to be properly compensated, on his thirty-mile route he should receive more money than would another rural mail courier with a route of fifty or sixty miles. The man in my vicinity may have to plow his own road a good part of the time in the winter months. When the snow is blowing he is not going to have good roads. On the other hand, on other routes the roads would be plowed and there would be no difficulty of this kind.
All these points must be considered. As the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) said this afternoon, I hope the committee will consider the requests of rural mail couriers from outlying districts. Not only should they appear from the Ottawa area; they should come from both the east and the west, so we may find out some of their difficulties. These will not be easily solved. It is my view, however, that in setting up a committee we are going about it in the right way.
If I understood the Postmaster General correctly, the bill introduced this afternoon will not become law until after the committee has made its recommendations. If it were to go through in its present form I am afraid it would prove to be only a temporary solution. While I am very much in favour of an upward adjustment of the fees or remuneration of rural mail couriers, I feel there must be safeguards. These will have to be considered by the committee and dealt with in its recommendations. Not only must there be safeguards for the couriers; there must be safeguards for the public as well. At the moment I have on my desk a petition in this connection. I have in mind a case where the regular mail delivery is on Wednesday but, because of a storm, the roads are impassable. Then Thursday is a holiday. Friday is another stormy day, with the result that the people in that area have received only one mail delivery that week instead of three. This is not uncommon.
In some areas the delivery is daily. Yet there are other areas just as thickly populated, and entitled to just as good delivery, where they have only three deliveries in a week. The committee will have to get to the bottom
Committee on Post Office of these conditions. As was suggested by the hon. member for Peel, it would be preferable to have a percentage of the witnesses come to Ottawa. They could be chosen from various areas across the country, and permitted to tell their story to the committee.
I could make some comments about discrimination, and many other subjects. However, after having listened to other hon. members who have spoken in the debate I think there is no need to repeat what they have said. I can state, briefly, that I am very much in favour of setting up the committee, and I express the hope that it will go into the situation thoroughly. I am of the opinion that the Postmaster General is looking for a solution. Having talked with him I am satisfied that he is sincere in this matter, and that he wishes to bring down legislation which will remedy the conditions from which the rural mail couriers are suffering. It is imperative that they be treated fairly in the matter of the compensation to which they are entitled.
I believe that is all I wish to say, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay the proceedings of the house for more than two or three minutes, because I feel that everything that could be said on this subject was said this afternoon. The debate will have shown the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) the arduous task ahead of the committee in separating the wheat from the chaff.
Excellent ideas have been put forth in the debate. I think all hon. members representing rural constituencies owe a debt of gratitude to the minister for setting up the committee. I do not think there is one of us who is not worried over the inequalities of the present system. Each of us has in the back of his mind some solution to overcome those inequalities; indeed, we have heard them discussed today.
I trust the present system will be superseded by one that will give the rural mail couriers a fair return on their investment, a fair return on the amount they put into their cars and equipment, or the sleighs they may have to use in the winter months. I trust some formula can be devised, based upon the length of the route, the number of boxes along the route, the condition of the roads and the like. When a man seeks a contract or is given the duty of delivering the mails he will then be assured of at least an honest and fair return on the amount he must lay out for equipment and for the time he must spend at his work.
Urban mail carriers are required to pass a civil service examination. As far as the

Committee on Post Office appointment of rural mail couriers is concerned, I think we should do away with the objectionable patronage that enters into these appointments and have civil service examinations set for these people, bearing in mind always that they should receive an adequate return on their investment and for the time required to carry out their duties.

Mr. Speaker, on the subject of this resolution, to which I give my entire support, I wish to point out to the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote), inasmuch as this resolution, which relates to the functioning of the rural mail delivery, applies to my riding, first a deficiency in the rural mail delivery in the constituency of Gloucester and, secondly, a gross anomaly in the present system.
I said a deficiency. According to the figures in the last report, or the directory published last December by the Post Office Department, 9,721 family heads are served in my constituency by your department. Of this number, 782 family heads get postal service through rural mail delivery. We have only 7 rural routes in the vast county of Gloucester which is unquestionably the largest rural constituency in the whole province of New Brunswick.
As I say, we have only 7 rural routes and only 7 per cent of our postal population, if I may use such an expression, is served by rural mail delivery. That is, in my opinion, a deficiency, and that is why I do urge the hon. minister to pay special attention to Gloucester county whenever representations are made to him for the establishment of new rural routes or new rural mail delivery systems. Frankly we have been rather sadly neglected up to now, as can readily be ascertained by the department's own figures.
I therefore wish to call the minister's attention to the case of the Canobie district, to which I have already referred in a letter which I wrote him on November 24 last. I would call the minister's attention to the fact that in the Canobie area there is, at present, one district that enjoys rural mail delivery. Now in this district there is one place called Springfield whose people have no service at all. There are no boxes in that district. There are 5 farmers, 5 families without any postal service at all. Moreover, there are in that same district 13 new settlement lots; this means that in the very near future there will be 18 farmers in the district of Springfield which, up to now, has had no postal service.
[Mr. Fulford.l

The same situation prevails in the western section of the Canobie district, known under the name of Doucetville. There is not a box at Doucetville. There are nonetheless between 10 and 12 good farmers without any postal service. The people from both Springfield and Doucetville must walk a distance of nearly a mile to get their mail in the boxes of neighbours who are charitable enough to allow the mail of these people who have no postal service to be deposited in their boxes.
In reply to my letter, the minister stated that my requests would receive serious consideration, but to date no decision has been made. I believe it is about time we had a formal decision from the department, so that we may know whether something can or cannot be done for those people who, I repeat, are without any service.
May I also bring to the minister's attention the very special case of two islands, Shippi-gan and Miscou islands, situated in the northwest part of my constituency. The situation there is quite unusual and, during certain periods of the year, especially in the spring and in the fall, mail services are completely inadequate. For those reasons I beg the minister to give special consideration to the matter when a request complying with the requirements set forth in the postal regulations is made to his department for the establishment of a rural mail service on Shippigan and Miscou islands.
There is another special case to which I want to draw the minister's attention; it is the case of the present post offices at Sormany, Nicholas Denys and Madran. These three post offices are located in a district which at present draws considerable attention from all those who are interested in the stock market across Canada, because they are located in the district where gigantic mining developments have taken place recently in the northern part of New Brunswick. I believe that in the near future requests will be made for the establishment of a rural mail delivery service in this new mining district and I do hope that the matter will be given special attention when that request is made.
There are other concrete cases which I would like to bring to the department's attention. I shall mention but one. It is the case of the new settlements of Allard-ville, D'Aulnay and St. Sauveur, where, as yet, no rural mail delivery service has been established; before long, a request will be submitted to the department to that effect.

I said there existed an anomaly in our district, and here it is. When I began these remarks I pointed out that, all told, 9,721 heads of families, according to the department's own figures, enjoyed postal service. Now 1,879 of these are English-speaking and 7,842 are French-speaking. That is to say that, taking the population of my constituency as a whole, 19-2 per cent are English-speaking and 80-8 per cent are French-speaking. Nevertheless rural mail delivery, which serves 782 heads of families, can be broken down thus: 443 English-speaking heads of families have it at present as against 339 that are French-speaking. That is to say that the current rural mail delivery system in the county of Gloucester serves English-speaking heads of families in the proportion of 56-6 per cent, whereas our French-speaking heads of families are served in the proportion of 43-4 per cent only.
Compare, Mr. Minister, this proportion or rather this disproportion with the figures I gave you a moment ago concerning the heads of families who are served by the postal services, and you will have there what I had reason to call, at the beginning of my remarks, an anomaly. I would therefore suggest that the department rectify, as soon as possible, this situation, which is quite abnormal, in the rural postal service of this great Acadian constituency of Gloucester in the province of New Brunswick.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to suggest to the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote), and any other members of the house who may want to be enlightened on the question of rural mail services, that they should consult Hansard of February 20, 1947. They will find there the remarks I made on that occasion, which I believe are as apt and to the point today as they were then. If the Postmaster General has actually read them I think he will agree with me. I see no purpose therefore in repeating or enlarging upon them, and if more hon. members would follow the same practice with respect to many other subjects I am sure our debates would be shortened.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word on this subject because I represent the largest constituency in area in the southern part of Ontario. It is sparsely settled in many districts, and I think there are at least as many rural mail routes as in any other constituency in the province. I have many grievances that I could air, but I do not like to thresh old straw. I do not think that does any good. I
Committee on Post Office have said before that I think the hiring of mail couriers should be done by the civil service commission, but there would be no use of my making that suggestion now or bringing forward a resolution to that effect because with the large number of Liberal members in the house I would not get very far with it.
The government has indicated the way it wants to handle this matter; and be that as it may, it cannot help but be an improvement over the old system. I realize that it gives the minister much more power than previously and much more opportunity for patronage, but even at that the situation cannot be any worse in the future than it has been in the past so far as my riding is concerned. I think the minister knows something about it. Most of it took place before his term of office began. So far as patronage is concerned, I cannot find very much fault since he took over the portfolio. I was pleased when I heard the minister say that there was not going to be any favouritism or patronage as a result of the proposed legislation, and that so far as the rural mail carriers were concerned everything was going to be done as fairly and equitably as possible and for the benefit of Canada as a whole.
It is a big problem because Canada is a large nation and we have so many diversified areas. In my riding we have some mail routes that do not go off paved roads, whereas in some of the more sparsely settled areas the roads are very narrow, hilly and rocky, and in some places it is almost impossible to travel over them with a car. Some of the mail carriers have to keep a car for the summer and to provide horse-drawn vehicles in the winter months.
I understand that the committee is going to be set up to recommend to the minister ways and means to pay the rural mail carriers on an equitable and fair basis. That is a big job, and if the committee goes into every mail route in Canada it will not be finished its work by this time next year. It will have to set up some sort of system whereby it will deal with certain classes of roads.
I want to say to the minister that I believe in my riding we have the best group of mail carriers in Canada. In fact they could not be any better. We have people who have carried the mail for twenty years and have never missed a trip winter or summer, rain or shine. Not one letter or parcel has ever gone astray on these routes.
I think the policy of the government has been that when the four-year contract for a mail route expires the contractor gets a renewal provided he is satisfactory and

Committee on Post Office does not want any more money. However, that has not always taken place. Patronage has come into the picture. I can cite many cases, and I do not have to go out ot my own riding to do it. I hope that situation will be changed. When a man is satisfactory, does not ask for any more money and can produce a petition signed by every mailbox owner on his route indicating that they want him to have the route, I hope the department will pay attention to these things and will not listen to the president or chairman of the Liberal association in a little corner of the riding who will only take the department off on a downhill road that is no good for anybody.
Liberal chairmen always listen.

I hope they are listening in my riding tonight. They have been anything but fair, and I want to tell you that it has not done them any good. Every time you change a mail carrier don't forget that there are four or five other applicants for the contract. When you pick one the other three are dissatisfied, and that has happened on a couple of occasions in my riding. They displeased many more than three. I think that is something the minister should take into consideration, and I hope he will not be like his predecessor.
I came to Ottawa to see his predecessor one time not so very long ago, and I remained here for two days. During that period I called him on the phone at least every hour trying to get an appointment, but he was too busy. I told him if he was too busy to see me for five minutes I was going to put a placard on my back and walk up and down in front of the office until he would see me. Then he said he could talk to me on the phone for a minute. When I put my case to him over the phone he said, "Oh, my officials, my officials, my officials."
Three times?

I hope the minister will run his department and not let his officials run him down the hill. Sometimes they are all right and sometimes they are all wrong. That is not good for the government either.
There is another matter to which I should like to refer. The hon. member for Hastings South (Mr. Follwell) spoke today and said that he had obtained extensions of mail routes on the basis of three boxes to a mile. I was very glad to get that information, because just yesterday I received a letter from the minister's department turning down a request for service on the basis of three boxes to less than a mile. The letter said that government policy was four boxes to a mile. In the last few years I have received several letters

from the Post Office Department all stating that the basis was four boxes to a mile. Therefore I say now that patronage can be a bad thing, because apparently some ridings can get service on the basis of three boxes to a mile.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit me-
You sit down. I did not ask you any questions.

On a question of privilege, if I may be permitted to speak from this side of the house, I am sure the hon. member will recall-if he will look at Hansard he will see it-that I said I was of the opinion it was three to a mile. I said I did not know how many it was to the mile. I referred it to the Postmaster General. I did not get an answer from him but someone on the other side of the house said "three to a mile". The hon. member immediately said that it was four to a mile in his constituency.
I was the one who made the statement, and I have one that is three to the mile.
Patronage!

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Hastings South (Mr. Follwell) also went back to something that happened in 1930; but look at the young gentleman. He doesn't remember what happened in 1930, and I think he had to admit that before he finished his speech tonight.
Quite right.

Nevertheless I do believe there are certain places where they should accept three boxes to a mile. As a matter of fact there is a place in my riding where I would like to get a route at three boxes to a mile. That is desirable where elderly persons live, especially when the mail courier is willing to deliver that mail without any additional cost. It is something that should be considered.
I am not in favour of this bill having to do only with contracts under $1,000. If you are going to give the minister a bit of leeway, well, give him some leeway. Why stop at $1,000? Make it something worth while because most mail routes are over $1,000.

my hon. friend will allow me, I think there is a little confusion. We intend to do exactly what he desires, to readjust contracts not only under $1,000 but all contracts except those covered by section 29.

I am glad to have that explanation because over at Beaverton last September they took the mail contract away

from the fellow who had had it for sixteen years. He never missed a trip and never lost a letter, but they gave it to another fellow on a contract at practically the same price. The fellow who had it for sixteen years had it sixteen years too long at the price he was being paid; and the fellow who got it last September has had it too long at the price he is getting. I am going to have a talk with the minister about a little increase for that fellow, because I certainly think he needs it.
There has been a new set-up for mail distribution in about one-third of my riding since the minister took over his office. I want to say that we appreciate that very much. It is something I have been after for five long years, but I never got any place until we got the genial minister in the proper chair and in the proper job. He got busy and did something about it, and we have a better mail service in one-third of my riding than we have had since confederation.
There are some more improvements that should be made, and I spoke to the minister about them. He said that I should get the matter in shape and come over and talk to him about it. The improvements are not going to cost any more money; there are just a few little things that could be shaped up. When we get this bill through the house, get this legislation set up, and have all the information and advice that the committee can give, we will be able to chat about these things and probably get around to doing something about them.
I did want to go into deliveries of mail in the towns, and I was wondering how it would be set up. Is it to be according to the population of the towns, or revenue, or just what will it be when we get the two deliveries a day? For instance, in the town of Lindsay we had two deliveries until recently.

Order. The committee is being set up to consider the operation of the rural mail delivery service. I do not think the committee would have power to go into city deliveries, and in any event this resolution does not affect delivery within cities.

Mr. Speaker, I abide by your ruling. Nevertheless the hon. member for Hastings South went into letter deliveries in Belleville and the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) discussed deliveries on trains and airplanes.
I think if the hon. member had brought that to the attention of the Speaker, those hon. members would have been called to order.

It happened that you were not in the chair, sir.

I am sure that would not have made any difference.
I abide by your ruling, sir. I think if there is any change it has to be a change for the better, and I am glad to say that I am in favour of the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly not my intention to follow the hon. gentleman who preceded me in all the political matters about which he spoke. My comment will be very brief because some of the points I had intended to make have already been covered by my colleague the member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier).
One point I would like to submit for the consideration of the committee that will be set up is the fact that sometimes we meet with difficulties when we try to obtain a rural route in some of the villages in my constituency. It would appear to me that when the Postmaster General has to make a decision regarding a mail route it must be determined whether the locality concerned is to be considered a rural region or an urban region. At Ste. Anne de Beaupre, a town in my riding, we have a community that is considered to be an urban district, yet closer to the village there is what is considered to be a rural district. The department claim that under the present regulations they do not qualify as an urban area.
May I suggest that some scheme could be arrived at, or some system of delivery, which would be neither a rural courier's route nor a city service, but something in between. I hope the regulations which will be established will have such a degree of flexibility as to permit people who want a particular type of service to receive that service.
If the minister speaks now, he will close the debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is the most far-reaching and is indeed the final step in making the federal crown in Canada liable in tort for damages for which, were it a private person of full age and capacity, it would be liable in respect of a tort committed by a servant of the crown or in respect of a breach of duty attaching to the ownership, occupation, possession or control of property, or in respect of motor vehicle damages sustained by any person by reason of a motor vehicle owned by the crown. The bill also has other purposes to which I shall allude later, but its main purpose is to make the crown, in respect to the matters which I have mentioned, liable to the full extent to which it would be liable if it were a private person of full age and capacity.
It is appropriate, I think, in discussing the principle of this bill to link it with the history and the development of the rules governing claims against the crown for redress in those cases where a subject feels himself aggrieved. In their historic origin our courts were the king's courts which were created to hear and determine suits brought between subject and subject in accordance with the rules of the common law. Since these courts had been created by the king and, in a very real sense, represented the monarchy in the exercise of its judicial function, it was not possible for a subject to sue the king in the king's own courts.
However, once in a while even in those times, subjects had legal claims against the crown for which their only hope of redress was by petitioning the king for justice. Since these petitions involved points of law which the king was not in a position to consider personally, the practice grew up under which he authorized certain courts to consider whether such petitions should be granted, by an order or fiat addressed to his own courts directing in effect: Let justice be done. It was only in this way that issues between the crown and subjects were brought before the courts and there determined in accordance with the rules of the common law.
It was thus that two principles emerged, the first of which was that claims might be asserted against the crown in the form of a petition; the second of which was that such claims could not be entertained until a flat had first been granted. These principles of the English common law were first given statutory form in Canada by this parliament in 1876 when Hon. Edward Blake, the minister of justice under the Alexander Mackenzie government, introduced the Petition of Right Act of Canada to that effect. Until this government introduced a bill in 1951

to abolish the flat, the granting of it continued to be the sole basis upon which petitions of right against His Majesty in the right of Canada could be decided in this country.
Although certain claims might be asserted against the crown in this way, the crown was very far from being in the same position as a private individual in respect of its subjects' claims generally. The only claims that could be made the subject matter of a petition of right were those in which the land, goods or money of the subject were in the possession of the crown or in which the claim arose out of a contract entered into by or on behalf of the crown.
That was the position in 1887 when this parliament enacted that the Exchequer Court of Canada, which had previously been established as the court in which laws relating to taxes and revenues might be enforced, should also be the appropriate forum for the hearing of these petitions of right. This legislation of 1887 also introduced a fundamental change in the law. Prior to that time, as I have said, claims against the crown arose where the lands, goods or money of the subject were in the possession of the crown, or arose out of a contract entered into by or on behalf of the crown. Claims against the crown could not be brought in respect of any tort-that is any wrongful act-not involving a breach of contract for which a civil action would lie. The reason an action could not be brought in respect of a tort or wrong was upon the ground that in law the king could do no wrong and therefore could not be liable in tort. But this act of 1887 gave the exchequer court jurisdiction to hear and determine every claim against the crown arising out of any debt, injury to the person or to the property, or any public work resulting from the negligence of any officer or servant of the crown while acting within the scope of his duties or employment.
Thus for the first time in Canada-and to the great credit of Canada, for the first time in the English-speaking world-actions in tort based upon the one tort of negligence only were permitted to be taken against the crown. I think that it is fitting that for this enlightened legislation we should pay our respects to Hon. John Thompson who was the minister of justice under Sir John A. Macdonald, and who subsequently became Sir John Thompson and prime minister himself.
As an indication of the enlightened attitude of Canada in this respect, it may be noted that it was not until 60 years later that the
Crown Liability
United Kingdom and other commonwealtl countries permitted proceedings against ths sovereign for torts.
With slight amendments from time to time this rule established in 1887 has prevailec until the present day. Actions against th< crown in tort are still confined to negligent although, as I pointed out on a previou: occasion, to say only that they are so con fined may to the layman be misleading as t( their scope unless one points out that a largi percentage of actions in tort-possibly as higl as between 90 and 95 per cent-are action; based upon the negligence of servants of thi crown.
In Canada the law as amended by thi; legislation of 1887 continued substantial!: without change until 1950, when this govern ment introduced the Statute Law Amendmen Act by which it was provided that action might be brought against crown corporation in the provincial courts. This legislation ii itself was a radical departure from existin; law and existing legal theory; for before tha time legal proceedings against the crown ii the right of Canada could only be taken in thi courts of His or Her Majesty in the right o Canada. The 1950 act therefore, in permittinj actions against the crown in the right o Canada to be taken in the courts of Hi Majesty in the right of the provinces, mad' these crown corporations amenable to th jurisdiction of all Canadian courts in mucl the same way as ordinary corporations.
In the following year, 1951, by an amend ment to the Petition of Right Act wi abolished the necessity of securing a fia before proceedings could be brought agains the crown. Proceedings may now be take] against the crown as of right and withou first obtaining the crown's consent.
The bill now before you represents per haps the most far-reaching change of al. Its purpose is to place the crown, in so fa as actions in tort are concerned, in substan tially the same position as a private indi vidual. Upon the passage of this bill th crown will be liable not only for all tort committed by agents or servants of th crown, but also for torts that may be com mitted without the intervention of a servan or agent, namely torts arising out of thi ownership, occupation, possession or contrc of property including motor vehicles. Th list of actions that are generally recognize' as coming within the classification of "torts are as follows: (a) negligence; (b) nuisance (c) trespass; (d) assault; (e) false imprie onment and false arrest; (f) malicious prose cution; (g) libel and slander; (h) deceit; (:

Crown Liability
interference with contract rights; (j) trover and conversion; (k) slander of title; (1) infringement of patent.
Making the crown liable for torts committed by its servants will make the crown liable for those torts I have just mentioned wherever they are committed by a servant while acting within the scope of his duties. Of these as I have already stated, the tort of negligence is the most significant, and next to it that of nuisance.
The extension of the crown's liability for breach of duty arising out of ownership, possession or control of property would make the crown liable as occupier to invitees, licensees and occasional trespassers in accordance with the ordinary rules of law; it would extend to the crown liability for nuisance or negligence committed otherwise than through the medium of a servant of the crown. For example, the crown would be under a duty to prevent injury to adjoining property from a building, from the escape of noxious and dangerous things, from the presence of dangerous things, from interference with riparian rights and, generally, for nuisance and negligence in respect of the management of crown property.
In the above respects Canada is now extending the liability of the crown in Canada in the same manner in which the United Kingdom has extended the liability of the crown in the United Kingdom.
At this point I think I should interject some words of reassurance to the taxpayers of this country. While these provisions will probably result in some increase in the amount payable by the crown to persons injured, it should be noted that many of the claims which will arise under this present legislation are now being paid on an ex gratia basis, notwithstanding that there is no legal liability, because it has been felt that there is a moral one. Therefore it is not expected that the total liability from a financial point of view will be increased too greatly. It is not expected, for example, that the liability of the crown in respect of all the new causes of action against the crown which are created by this bill will be anything like as great financially as those based upon the negligence of the crown's servants.
There would, of course, be no liability in any case where anything was done under the authority of a statute. Nor is it intended to impose liability in respect of the ownership of property unless the crown is, in fact, controlling and administering the property. For example, in the Northwest Territories, and to a lesser extent in the provinces, the federal crown owns wild or unoccupied lands. In respect of such lands it is intended to make

the crown liable only where the crown has, in fact, assumed control and is in some way using or administering the property.
It is also proposed to exclude liability where the crown has abandoned the use of a particular work. For example, the crown might, as a public convenience, construct a wharf in a remote area but, because the need for it no longer exists, the crown might cease to maintain it. It is intended to make provision for a public declaration of abandonment in order that the crown would not be obliged either to continue to maintain the work indefinitely or to demolish it.
This brings me to the second main provision of the bill, which is that it makes applicable to the crown the ordinary laws relating to salvage services rendered in assisting any crown ships or in saving life therefrom or in saving any cargo or apparel belonging to the crown, in the same manner as if the ship, cargo or apparel belonged to a private person. Here again this provision is a counterpart of that contained in the United Kingdom crown proceedings act.
The third main provision of this bill is that permitting small claims in negligence up to a limit of $1,000 to be taken in the district or county courts that would have jurisdiction if the action were between subjects. This will enable the issue to be determined locally and result in a saving of costs, and will enable small negligence claims to be disposed of quickly. All other actions of course will continue to be brought in the Exchequer Court of Canada.
May I say in conclusion that the step being taken in this bill follows logically from the development of our whole legal history and particularly from the measures which we enacted in this present parliament in 1950 and 1951. In all these matters we have to keep in mind two important factors. On the one hand there is the obvious consideration that the citizen as a litigant should have an economical and effective method of pursuing his claim against the crown. Against this must be balanced, however, an equally important consideration, namely that in the interests of the general body of citizens as taxpayers this litigation against the crown should be carried on as economically and efficiently as possible.
This is the third important piece of legislation in this regard which the government has brought forward in the last three years. We have gone into this process gradually in order to make sure step by step that we were providing reforms for the litigant without imposing any undue burdens upon the taxpayer. Our experience with the legislation which we passed in 1950 and again in 1951

in this respect has been very favourable. Our impression is that the present legislation will remove virtually all of the restrictions upon litigants who desire to sue the crown without imposing a new and costly burden upon the taxpayer.

Mr. Speaker, I would move the adjournment of the debate and would suggest that, in view of the fact that the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) will not be here tomorrow, it might stand over until the beginning of the week.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I might have the consent of the house to revert to motions for a couple of moments, I would be glad to announce to you, to the house and to the country that collective bargaining is still an effective instrument to deal with labour relations in this country.
The representatives of the Canadian railways and the representatives of the brotherhood who had been negotiating for some considerable time to settle the renewal and revision of the collective agreement governing their relations have agreed upon terms for the renewal and revision of that agreement; and the instructions that the members of the union would withdraw from service at six o'clock on the 2nd of February are being cancelled at this moment. The railways are also withdrawing the notices of embargoes on shipments of perishable goods.
I think it would be appropriate to add- and I feel that this would be in the name of all the members of this House of Commons- that we are highly appreciative of the publicspiritedness of those who have been negotiating on behalf of the railways and on behalf of the brotherhood. They have fully and magnificently recognized their responsibilities to the Canadian people whose servants they are, as we are, and whose interests are as dear to them as they are to us and to those we represent.
I think they have done a magnificent job, and that it is a credit to Canadian democracy that matters about which there were honest and sincere and pretty widely diverging views could be settled when honest men of good will got together and did their best to discharge their responsibilities to their fellow citizens.
Threatened Railway Strike
That has been done; and I think it is a bright page to be written into the history of labour relations in this country.
May I ask the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) if he is in a position to give us, in general, the terms of the settlement arrived at?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would prefer that that should come from those who have made the settlement. It has been their responsibility, and they have discharged it magnificently.
I can say that there are two points which have been mentioned to me, that perhaps had to be mentioned to me. One was that there is an increase of the order of 12 per cent going into force, with an appropriate retroactive date to be determined by the parties.
There is for a certain group of yardmen, I believe it is, a forty-hour week, to go into effect on the 1st of October next, evidently with adjustments which will have to be made in the wage scale so that the take-home pay will not be seriously affected by that change in the hours.
The adjustments with respect to the application of the forty-hour week are matters upon which there still remain diverging views on the part of the representatives of the men and the representatives of the company. They have both agreed that I am personally-not as Prime Minister, not as head of the government'-but that I am personally to select a person to decide, as referee, what those adjustments will be, both parties agreeing to abide by the decisions of that referee.
As that is a matter which will not require to be implemented before October 1, 1953, both parties told me that there was no immediate urgency in announcing the referee, but that they hoped it might be done within a reasonable time. I was naturally highly flattered by the confidence they both expressed.
I asked them if they had any suggestions. They preferred to make no suggestions, but to leave it entirely to me to make the selection, without any suggestions or recommendations or objections. They said they preferred to have me use my own best judgment in selecting a person to do that for them, and that they were going to be satisfied to abide by whatever adjustment that referee decided was the proper adjustment in the circumstances.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we of this group would like to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in the well-deserved tribute which he paid to the parties who have carried on

Threatened Railway Strike these negotiations, and who have shown the public spirit to which the Prime Minister referred tonight.
I am sure we are all delighted, not only that an agreement has been reached but that it has been reached through the process of collective bargaining, without any outside interference. That is perhaps the most important aspect of the announcement made tonight by the Prime Minister, and we applaud it very happily. We are naturally interested-and I think that goes for all of us-in the details of the settlement. I was afraid at first, when the Prime Minister began to reply to the question of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), that he would not be able to give us any of the terms tonight. However, he has been able to give us a good deal of information.
That information does seem to suggest that a basis of settlement agreeable to both sides has been worked out. I wonder if the Prime Minister is in a position to say whether or not the terms agreed upon include any reference to the changes in rules which did, for a long time, stand in the way of a settlement. Is that subject in the category of matters that have been agreed upon, or is it in the category of matters to be dealt with oy the person whom the Prime Minister will name?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The only matter to be dealt with by the referee I am to appoint is the matter of adjustment required by the institution of the forty-hour week. There are other matters about which precise decisions have not been arrived at, but the parties have agreed that they trust each other sufficiently to be able to work those out without there being any danger of their interfering with the completion of a collective agreement.
